cultivar: Menghai large-leaf (Menghai dayezhong) and other Yunnan assamica populations
processing: Sun-dried raw pu-erh maocha from across the county, usually blended across villages, grades and sometimes years, then steamed and pressed into cakes or bricks under hydraulic or stone presses.
harvest_season: Spring for the premium lots; factory blends draw on spring, summer and autumn leaf and are released through the year.
appearance_dry: Mixed grades of dark-green to brown twisted leaf with a scattering of golden buds, pressed into a firm, even cake.
appearance_liquor: Golden-orange when young, deepening to reddish amber over a decade, usually clear.
appearance_wet: Medium to large leaves of uneven size and colour, showing the blend, with a few reddish edges.
taste_profile: Full and robust: a frank bitterness, grip on the tongue, honey and dried-grass sweetness underneath and a long warming finish; the heavier, deeper 'Menghai flavour' as opposed to the lighter Lincang style.

brewing.notes: Rinse once (twice for a tightly pressed factory cake). Break the cake along the layers rather than stabbing through it, so the leaves stay whole; tight factory pressing needs a longer first steep to open.

vintage_note: Menghai sheng is the backbone of the dated-cake market: factory cakes carry a production year and batch number, boutique cakes a spring harvest year. Young means 1–3 years, mid-aged roughly 5–15, and 'aged' usually implies pre-2005 production; the late-1980s and 1990s Menghai Tea Factory cakes are the reference for aged sheng, while the 2003–2007 boom years produced the enormous volume of mid-aged tea you see offered today. Everything from 2005 to 2025 is readily available; the price gap between a Kunming-dry and a Guangdong-wet example of the same batch is real and worth asking about.
description:
Menghai County, west of Jinghong in Xishuangbanna, is where most of the famous raw pu-erh of the last eighty years was pressed. It contains Bulang Shan, Nannuo, Hekai, Bada, Mengsong and Pasha, and it is home to the Menghai Tea Factory, founded in 1940 as the Fohai Tea Factory, whose numbered recipes defined what a 'standard' cake tastes like. When a cake just says Menghai, it usually means a blend from several of these areas rather than a single hillside.

The county grows a large-leaf population known as Menghai dayezhong, thick and oily, that gives tea with more bitterness, more body and more staying power than the gentler leaf of Lincang or Yiwu. Factory production blends grades and villages for consistency, presses tightly, and aims at a tea that will taste the same next year and better in ten.

The cup is robust: honest bitterness, some grip, honey and hay sweetness underneath and a long warm finish that Chinese drinkers call 'Menghai wei', the Menghai flavour. Young factory cakes are rougher than boutique gushu, which is the point: they are built to age. Brew them a little heavier and give tight compression a longer first steep; a well-made blend improves across the session rather than peaking at steep three.

It is sold by production year and, for the factories, by recipe number (7542 and 8582 are the sheng classics) or by named product. Single-village Menghai tea is sold under the village name instead. Look for the pressing date on the wrapper and the batch code; a 'Menghai' cake at a suspiciously low price with a famous village name on it is almost always a county-wide blend with a borrowed name.

A good way to learn the county is to drink a young factory cake next to a single-village Nannuo or Bulang from the same year: you will taste what blending buys (balance, depth) and what it costs (clarity).
history:
Menghai is a county in Xishuangbanna, and as a tea name it usually points to the county's factory blends rather than one hillside. Its reputation rests largely on the Menghai Tea Factory.

The factory registered the Dayi trademark in 1989 and restructured into a company during the 1990s. Its raw recipe 7542 has been its largest-volume raw cake, consistent enough over decades that the market treats it as a yardstick for price and quality.
